name: Simulated Clinical Trials
title: Simulated Clinical Trials
answer: Simulated clinical trials use computational models to estimate how a treatment might behave in people before, alongside, or instead of some parts of a physical trial. They cover virtual patients, synthetic control arms, dose selection, trial design, and safety signal exploration. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models and 797 scientific models, and this topic sits where those two groups meet. The work is not a replacement for all human evidence, it is a way to test assumptions, prioritize candidates, and reduce the number of people exposed to ineffective or harmful regimens.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: It runs on a mix of mechanistic simulation engines, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic models, quantitative systems pharmacology platforms, and machine learning surrogates. These workloads need compute for large virtual populations, often on cloud clusters with GPUs for neural models and CPUs for ordinary differential equation solvers. Data infrastructure includes electronic health records, historical trial data, real world data, and synthetic patient generators, all held in governed pipelines. Reproducibility depends on versioned code, containerized environments, and traceable input datasets.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Teams start by defining the clinical question and the target patient population, then build or select a model that links drug exposure to biomarkers, endpoints, or adverse events. They calibrate the model against prior trials and biological data, then run thousands of virtual patients across dose levels and schedules. Sensitivity analysis and external validation check whether the model behaves sensibly outside its training conditions. Results are reported with uncertainty intervals and assumptions, not as a single predicted outcome.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Simulated trials raise questions about data rights, patient consent, model provenance, and the evidence standard regulators will accept. A simulation can encode bias from historical trials, so teams document data sources, inclusion criteria, and known gaps. The site's 215 compliance and regulation pages reflect how much of this field depends on audit trails, validation reports, and clear labeling of simulated versus observed results. Liability can follow if a simulation is used to support a claim about safety or effectiveness without adequate disclosure.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Regulators and sponsors are exploring how simulated evidence can support certain regulatory decisions, especially for dose selection and trial enrichment. The field is moving toward digital twins of patients, multiscale models that connect molecular effects to organ level outcomes, and continuous updating as new trial data arrives. Wider adoption will depend on transparent validation, shared benchmarks, and agreement on when a simulation is strong enough to change a trial or reduce a control arm. The likely near term role is augmentation, not wholesale replacement of randomized human trials.
